species.note: This catalog's first Hypoestes. NC State lists common names alphabetically, so its page opens with "Baby's Tears" — a name that belongs to Soleirolia soleirolii everywhere else — so land this as Polka Dot Plant and let no Soleirolia care text leak in. Capture the non-toxic statement with its exact cat/dog (and horse) scoping rather than a genus-level claim, and resist soil_drainage fast: that value is only for sharp or sandy drainage with no wet tolerance. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This would be the catalog's third Peperomia after argyreia and obtusifolia, so every field must be species-specific rather than reused from those records. "Ripple Peperomia", "Silver Heart" and "Little Fantasy" are cultivar-driven aliases — take no care or size data from cultivar pages, and capture the non-toxic-to-cats-and-dogs statement exactly as scoped. Do not mark soil_drainage fast; this wants a well-drained but moisture-holding mix, not sharp drainage. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

The catalog already holds Tradescantia zebrina under "Spiderwort / Inch Plant", so lead this one with Purple Heart and keep the two records from sharing text. Its alias list includes "Moses in the Basket", which properly belongs to Tradescantia spathacea, and "Purple Spiderwort" — do not let either pull in a sibling's content. Capture the sap contact-dermatitis handling warning separately from the cat-and-dog ingestion toxicity rather than collapsing the two. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Thaumatophyllum, and NC State still files the page under philodendron-bipinnatifidum (the Thaumatophyllum slug 301-redirects there) — expect Philodendron selloum and P. bipinnatifidum as synonyms across sources. Its alias list includes both "Heartleaf Philodendron", already landed here as Philodendron hederaceum, and "Panda Plant", so land it as Tree Philodendron / Split Leaf Philodendron and source nothing from the hederaceum record. Capture the calcium-oxalate toxicity with its cat/dog scoping plus any human handling or sap-irritation warning stated separately. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

The corpus already holds Sedum ternatum and Hylotelephium spectabile under "Showy Stonecrop", so do not land this on the bare alias "Stonecrop" — lead with Burro's Tail. This is one of the few entries where soil_drainage fast is genuinely right, but only if the page calls for sharp or sandy drainage with no wet tolerance; capture any non-toxic statement with its exact cat/dog scoping and the warning that the leaves shatter off on handling. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

The catalog's only Goeppertia is orbifolia, landed under the bare common name "Calathea", so land this one as Peacock Plant and keep the two records from sharing care or humidity text. Watch the Calathea-to-Goeppertia rename — the calathea-makoyana slug redirects to goeppertia-makoyana, and older sources still say Calathea makoyana. Set moisture_retentive only if the page states consistently moist soil as a cultivation requirement, not as a preference, and capture the non-toxic-to-cats-and-dogs statement exactly as scoped. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Cordyline. Its alias list runs to "Cabbage Palm" and "Cabbage Tree", names that belong to Cordyline australis and Sabal palmetto elsewhere, so lead with Ti Plant and import care from neither. Capture the saponin toxicity with its cat-and-dog scoping, and record any statement about tap-water fluoride or salt sensitivity as a cultivation note rather than folding it into watering. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

The corpus already holds Kalanchoe blossfeldiana, so build every field from this species' own page rather than reusing the florist kalanchoe's record. "Panda Plant" is also listed as an alias of Philodendron bipinnatifidum, so name the genus in any disambiguation text; capture the cardiac-glycoside toxicity with its exact cat/dog scoping instead of a genus-wide claim. Use soil_drainage fast only if the page specifies sharp or sandy drainage with no wet tolerance. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

Genus is already in the corpus four times (Salvia officinalis as Sage, S. rosmarinus, S. splendens as Scarlet Sage, S. yangii as Russian Sage), so lead with Woodland Sage and do not let culinary-sage or Russian-sage content bleed in. The big trap is that nursery plants tagged 'May Night' and 'Caradonna' are frequently the hybrid Salvia × sylvestris (S. nemorosa × S. pratensis) — take nothing from a sylvestris, superba, or verticillata page. It wants good drainage but grows in ordinary garden loam, so reserve soil_drainage fast for a sharp or sandy requirement. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Stachys; older sources use the synonyms Stachys lanata and Stachys olympica, and the sibling Stachys officinalis (Betony) is a wholly different garden plant whose page must not be used. 'Helen von Stein' / 'Big Ears' are cultivars, not sources. Toxicity is generally benign, but capture whether the page makes any edibility claim at all rather than assuming; drainage is the real requirement — it rots in wet ground, so fast is defensible only if the page specifies dry or sharp drainage, and moisture_retentive is wrong here. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Veronica; some floras place it as Pseudolysimachion spicatum, so the accepted-name check matters. Keep it clear of Veronica longifolia, the mat-forming creeping speedwells (V. prostrata, V. umbrosa 'Georgia Blue'), and especially Veronicastrum virginicum (Culver's Root), a different genus sold under overlapping 'speedwell' naming. It needs average, well-drained soil, so do not reach for soil_drainage fast unless the page states a sharp or sandy requirement. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

The corpus already has Papaver rhoeas as Corn Poppy, so guard against sibling bleed from rhoeas, P. somniferum, and P. nudicaule, and note that much of the trade's 'Oriental poppy' is P. bracteatum or hybrid stock. Toxicity is the thing to get exactly right: the milky latex carries alkaloids, so record the cat and dog scoping as the source states it, keep the sap-irritation handling warning as its own claim, and capture any explicit not-edible statement with its wording. It goes summer-dormant and rots in wet ground, so well-drained soil is a cultivation requirement and moisture_retentive must not be set. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Agastache; do not merge in Agastache rugosa (Korean mint) or the ubiquitous garden hybrid 'Blue Fortune' (A. rugosa × A. foeniculum), and note that true hyssop, Hyssopus officinalis, is an unrelated plant sharing the common name. Leaves and flowers are used for tea, so capture the edibility statement verbatim with whatever conditions the source attaches and do not generalize it to the hybrids or to Hyssopus. It wants dry to medium, well-drained soil; use fast only if sharp or sandy drainage is actually specified. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Platycodon; it was formerly Campanula grandiflora and the corpus already holds Campanula rotundifolia as Common Harebell, so the overlapping bellflower naming must not pull harebell content across, and watch for the epithet written as grandiflorum. The root is eaten in Korean cooking as doraji, so only record an edibility statement if this species page makes one, with its stated preparation conditions, plus any saponin or raw-root caution as written. It resents transplanting and wet winter soil, which is a drainage requirement rather than a case for moisture_retentive. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Lamium; the weedy siblings Lamium album, L. purpureum and L. amplexicaule share the dead-nettle name, and Lamiastrum galeobdolon (Yellow Archangel) is a different genus routinely shelved alongside it, so none of their pages may be used. Do not borrow anything from stinging nettle (Urtica), which is unrelated despite the name. Capture spread and invasiveness warnings as stated for this species specifically, and note that variegated cultivars like 'White Nancy' and 'Beacon Silver' carry cultivar-only advice. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Brunnera; it was previously Anchusa myosotidiflora, and the 'forget-me-not' common names it carries overlap with Myosotis, a different genus whose content must stay out. The hugely popular variegated cultivars ('Jack Frost', 'Looking Glass') come with cultivar-specific sun-scorch and reversion advice that does not belong in a species record. It is a shade plant with a genuine consistently-moist cultivation requirement, which is the case where moisture_retentive is legitimately earned. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

Tagetes patula is already landed as French marigold, so lead with African Marigold and keep the two records visibly distinct; be aware some authorities now sink T. patula into T. erecta, so confirm which accepted name the resolver returns before landing. Capture NC State's low-severity poison block exactly as written: phototoxic thiophene derivatives, contact dermatitis on handling, the named poison part, and any pet scoping, and record petal edibility only with the conditions the page states. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Antirrhinum; the dedicated page tags it non-toxic for cats, dogs and horses, so record that per-animal scoping verbatim rather than a blanket 'non-toxic'. It is sold as a cool-season annual but behaves as a short-lived perennial in mild zones, so set moisture_retentive only if a cultivation requirement actually demands consistently moist soil. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

Impatiens walleriana is landed as Impatiens, so lead with New Guinea Impatiens; the dedicated page notes the two are routinely confused, and this one tolerates far more sun, which is exactly the care difference worth capturing. It is tagged non-toxic for cats, dogs and horses — record that scoping exactly. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Jacobaea — it is the plant older labels and sources call Senecio cineraria, and the corpus already carries a Senecio-lineage entry (String of Bananas, landed as Curio radicans), so resolve the accepted name before landing. Toxicity here is unusually specific and must be captured piece by piece: all parts toxic if ingested with possible serious liver damage, brief minor skin irritation on contact, and an explicit gloves-and-protective-clothing handling warning, with pet scoping only as the page states it. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

Pelargonium × hortorum is landed as Annual Geranium, so lead with Ivy Geranium and keep the trailing basket type distinct from the upright zonal; the true Geranium genus (maculatum, sanguineum) is separately landed and must not be conflated with either. The poison block is low severity — mild contact (allergic) dermatitis with a named poison part — so record the handling detail and the stated severity rather than a general 'toxic'. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Calendula; the dedicated pages also list Common Marigold, which will collide with the landed Tagetes patula (French marigold) unless the record leads with Pot Marigold. Edibility is stated for the flowers only — slightly bitter, tangy and peppery, used in salads and as a dye — so capture that condition precisely, keep the non-toxic-for-cats-and-dogs scoping exactly as tagged, and do not extend edibility to the rest of the plant. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Angelonia; its alternate common name Summer Snapdragon will collide with Antirrhinum majus if that also lands, so lead with Angelonia and note the resemblance only in prose. It is a heat- and drought-tolerant bedding plant, so reserve soil_drainage fast for an explicit sharp or sandy drainage requirement with no wet tolerance, and set moisture_retentive only on a stated cultivation requirement. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Gomphrena; the dedicated page lists Batchelor's Button among its common names, which collides with the landed Centaurea cyanus (Bachelor's Button), so lead with Globe Amaranth. Amaranthus tricolor is landed as Joseph's Coat and is a different genus despite the shared 'amaranth' — keep them apart, and take toxicity only from the dedicated page, leaving pet scoping unclaimed if it is silent. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Eruca. Main trap is the name: Eruca sativa is the synonym most seed packets use and it 404s on NC State, so land the record under Eruca vesicaria; the dedicated page's edibility statement is expansive (leaves, flowers, seed pods and seeds, harvested young before they turn tough and bitter) and those harvest conditions should be captured, not flattened to "edible." Soil texture spans clay through sand at Good Drainage/Moist, so this is not a soil_drainage fast case. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

The corpus already holds Cucurbita pepo as "Squash" and Cucurbita maxima as "Pumpkin," so lead with Butternut Squash and do not let either landed record's content stand in for this one. NC State's name list for moschata also includes bare "Squash" and "Crookneck Squash," the latter colliding with the summer squashes that belong to C. pepo. Page gives Full sun, high organic matter, neutral pH and Good Drainage, so no fast drainage and no moisture_retentive unless the page states it as a cultivation requirement. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Melissa. Watch the common-name collisions: NC State lists it as Balm, Balm Mint and Common Balm, which brush against landed Monarda didyma ("Bee Balm") and landed Mentha spicata ("Mint") in the same family, so lead with Lemon Balm. Edibility is scoped to leaves and flowers used in teas and flavorings; its reputation for self-seeding and spreading is a maintenance trait, not a water requirement, so do not set moisture_retentive off it. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

The corpus holds seven Brassica entries already, all of them oleracea groups plus Brassica rapa (Rapifera Group) turnip, so the trap is reusing Brassica oleracea cabbage-family content for what is a genuinely separate species. NC State's name list runs Brown Mustard, Chinese Mustard, Giant Red Mustard, Indian Mustard and Leaf Mustard, so pick the leading common name off the dedicated page rather than the packet. Edibility covers leaves, seeds, flowers and stems raw or cooked, with a 3-5 day refrigerated storage condition worth keeping. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Physalis. Physalis ixocarpa is the synonym in wide circulation and it 404s on NC State, while Physalis peruviana and Physalis pruinosa are different ground-cherry species with no page here, so keep them out of the record. Toxicity is the thing to capture exactly: the page marks the plant both Edible and Poisonous, with solanine and other solanidine alkaloids in flowers, fruits, leaves and stems while mature fruits are edible whole, so record the ripeness condition rather than a blanket edible or a blanket toxic claim, and keep any cat/dog scoping the page states. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

Landed Origanum vulgare is "Oregano," so lead with Sweet Marjoram and keep the two records distinct; NC State also lists "Pot Marjoram" among majorana's names even though that name usually points at Origanum onites, so do not follow it. Edibility is leaves and flowers in tea and as a flavoring, harvested before the flowers open. Soil is loam, sand and shallow rocky at neutral-to-alkaline pH with Good Drainage, which is still Good Drainage, so reserve soil_drainage fast for a page that actually calls for sharp or sandy drainage with no wet tolerance. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

Landed Allium schoenoprasum is "Chives" and landed Allium porrum is "Leek," and NC State lists "Wild Leek" among this species' names, so lead with Garlic Chives and keep it off both landed records. Toxicity needs both halves recorded: sulfides with poison parts flowers, fruits, leaves, roots, seeds and stems, sitting alongside an edibility statement for leaves, bulbs and flowers that the page itself qualifies with a dose-and-part caveat, so keep that caveat's conditions rather than resolving it to edible or toxic, and note the pet scoping the page gives. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

Landed Prunus avium is "Sweet Cherry" and landed Prunus serrulata is the ornamental "Japanese Flowering Cherry," so lead with Sour Cherry and do not inherit either record's fruiting or size content. Toxicity to capture exactly: cyanide in leaves, seeds and stems, with the page's specific carve-outs that a couple of accidentally swallowed pits will not cause poisoning, that crushed or chewed seeds are considerably worse, and the warning about blending unpitted fruit. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

title: home-landscape shrubs, hedges, small trees and climbers

species.note: The corpus already holds H. macrophylla, H. paniculata and the climbing H. anomala subsp. petiolaris, so keep every fact scoped to quercifolia and never borrow bigleaf-hydrangea bloom-color/pH lore, which does not apply here. Capture the hydrangea toxicity precisely as the pages state it (cyanogenic glycoside in leaves, buds, flowers and bark; ASPCA scoping to cats, dogs and horses) rather than a generic 'toxic' claim, and watch the drainage enum: this species wants moist but well-drained soil and resents wet feet, which is a preference, not a moisture_retentive cultivation requirement. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

Distinguish it from the three landed hydrangeas by name and by habit: it blooms on new wood, unlike H. macrophylla, and the ubiquitous 'Annabelle' is a cultivar, so do not let cultivar pages supply the species record. Record the same cyanogenic-glycoside toxicity with its explicit cat/dog/horse scoping and its poison-part list, and note that although it takes more moisture than most shrubs, moisture_retentive belongs only if a page states moist soil as a cultivation requirement rather than a tolerance. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Syringa. Traps: 'lilac' is also attached to unrelated plants (chinaberry, summer lilac Buddleja davidii, which is already landed as Butterfly Bush), so reject any fact sourced under that loose common name, and note that most garden lilacs sold are S. vulgaris cultivars or S. x hybrida crosses. Toxicity is the reverse of the usual pattern here — lilac is generally reported non-toxic to people and pets and the flowers are described as edible — so capture that statement exactly as written with any conditions attached, and do not mark soil_drainage fast just because the species demands good drainage and neutral-to-alkaline soil. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

The corpus holds only the upright Juniperus virginiana, so keep habit facts separate: this is the prostrate groundcover juniper ('Blue Rug', 'Wiltonii') and its mature size, spacing and pruning limits differ entirely. Capture the handling side of toxicity exactly — foliage contact dermatitis and sap irritation warnings, plus whatever the pages say about berry-like cones and pets — and note this is a legitimate soil_drainage fast case if the pages describe sandy, sharply drained, drought-tolerant siting with no wet tolerance. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

The corpus has only Euonymus alatus (Burning Bush), and the two share nothing but a genus, so do not carry over deciduous-shrub facts to this evergreen vine-shrub; also watch that 'wintercreeper' and 'euonymus' get used loosely for E. japonicus in trade listings. Capture toxicity with its part scoping (fruit and seeds the main concern, with cat/dog statements as the source words them) and record the invasive-status and climbing-by-rootlet behavior, since several states list it; a plant that both spreads as groundcover and climbs is a real care-advice distinction. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

Taxus baccata (English Yew) is landed, so the sibling confusion is the main trap: most American hedge yews are actually the hybrid Taxus x media (Anglojap Yew), and its pages must not be used to fill this species record. Toxicity must be captured with unusual precision — taxine alkaloids in foliage, bark and seed are lethal to people, dogs, cats, horses and livestock, while the fleshy red aril itself is the one part usually described as non-toxic; record that edibility caveat exactly as the source words it, seed included. Yews demand good drainage and die in wet soil, but that alone is not soil_drainage fast unless the page describes sharp or sandy drainage. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Chaenomeles. Traps: it is confused with true quince (Cydonia oblonga) and with the shorter C. japonica, and nursery tags often say only 'flowering quince'. Two things must be captured verbatim — the fruit is described as edible only when cooked (jellies and preserves), which is an edibility statement with a condition, and the stems are thorny, so the handling warning belongs in the record alongside any pet-toxicity scoping. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

Three native viburnums are landed (dentatum, nudum, prunifolium), all with different common names and uses, so scope every fact to carlesii and do not import arrowwood or blackhaw facts. Watch the hybrid trap: V. x burkwoodii and V. x juddii both have carlesii as a parent and are sold under overlapping fragrance claims. Record toxicity as the pages state it, including whether fruit is described as edible or only as wildlife food, with cat/dog scoping kept exact. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

title: bulbs, tubers, tender patio and Mediterranean plants

species.note: This catalog's first Caladium; NC State lists its common names alphabetically so the page opens on "Angel Wings" — the trade and Missouri Botanical name is simply Caladium, and "Elephant's Ears" appears there too, which collides with Colocasia and with the already-landed Alocasia × mortfontanensis 'Polly', so do not let elephant-ear text cross over; watch the synonym Caladium × hortulanum, under which most named strains are listed, and keep to the straight species page. Capture toxicity exactly: insoluble calcium oxalate raphides in all parts, ASPCA-toxic to cats, dogs and horses, plus the sap/handling irritation warning for dividing tubers. Enum trap: this wants consistently moist, humus-rich soil, so moisture_retentive is justified only if a page states it as a cultivation requirement, and soil_drainage must not be fast — there is no sharp/sandy-only claim here. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Muscari; the common name shares "hyacinth" with the landed Hyacinthus orientalis but this is a different genus with far smaller bulbs, so write nothing that reads as forced-bulb hyacinth care, and distinguish it from the siblings M. botryoides and M. neglectum which share the same trade name. Toxicity is bulb-centred — capture whatever the pages actually say about ingestion of bulbs and whether any cat/dog scoping is given, rather than importing generic Hyacinthus oxalate text. Enum trap: bulbs need drainage to avoid rot but the pages describe ordinary well-drained garden soil, so soil_drainage fast belongs only if a page states sharp or sandy drainage with no wet tolerance. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Zantedeschia; it is not a true lily, and NC State also lists it as "African Lily," which collides directly with Agapanthus — keep the two apart. Do not blend in the colored florist callas (Z. elliottiana, Z. rehmannii and their hybrids), which are a separate, tenderer group. Capture toxicity precisely: insoluble calcium oxalate raphides in all parts, ASPCA-toxic to cats, dogs and horses, with the sap dermatitis handling note. Enum trap: this species genuinely tolerates boggy margins and standing water, so moisture_retentive is defensible if a page frames wet soil as a cultivation requirement, and soil_drainage must never be fast. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Colocasia, and a name minefield: NC State's alphabetical common-name list opens with "Caladium" and also gives "Elephant Ears," both of which collide with Caladium bicolor, while the landed Xanthosoma sagittifolium (Tannia) is a near look-alike aroid — keep all three distinct and do not reuse each other's text. Toxicity and edibility must be captured together and exactly: insoluble calcium oxalate raphides make it ASPCA-toxic to cats, dogs and horses and irritating to handle, yet the corms and leaves are a staple food only when thoroughly cooked, so the edibility statement has to carry that condition verbatim. Enum trap: it grows in standing water and bog margins, so moisture_retentive is appropriate only where a page states wet soil as a cultivation requirement, and soil_drainage fast is flatly wrong. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Galanthus; the obvious confusion is Leucojum aestivum (summer snowflake), a different genus with a nearly identical white nodding flower, and the sibling G. elwesii is sold under the same "snowdrop" label. Capture toxicity exactly as stated: lycorine-type and galantamine alkaloids concentrated in the bulbs, ASPCA scoping for cats, dogs and horses, plus any warning about bulbs being mistaken for edible onion bulbs in storage. Enum trap: these want well-drained but humus-rich woodland soil that does not bake dry, so soil_drainage fast applies only if a page specifies sharp or sandy drainage with no wet tolerance. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

The genus is already in the corpus via Lilium longiflorum (Easter Lily), so this must be written fresh rather than adapted from that record, and the page carries "Previously known as Lilium tigrinum" — expect older sources under that name. The landed Hemerocallis fulva (Daylily) is the other orange roadside lily-shaped plant and is a different family entirely; do not let them blur. Toxicity has to be scoped with real care: true Lilium species cause acute, potentially fatal kidney failure in cats specifically, including from pollen and vase water, while dogs typically show only gastrointestinal upset — state the cat-versus-dog difference exactly as the source does rather than a generic "toxic to pets." Enum trap: lily bulbs rot in wet ground but the pages describe ordinary well-drained garden soil, so soil_drainage fast needs an explicit sharp or sandy claim with no wet tolerance. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Agapanthus; NC State also lists it as "African Lily," which is exactly what Zantedeschia aethiopica is called there, so guard against the collision, and note that most plants sold are subsp. orientalis while the name Agapanthus africanus is used loosely in the trade for material that is usually this species. Capture toxicity specifically: the sap contains irritant saponins that can cause mouth and throat ulceration if chewed and skin irritation when the fleshy roots and leaves are cut, so record the handling warning alongside whatever cat/dog scoping the source gives. Enum trap: it is drought-tolerant once established and resents winter wet, but soil_drainage fast still requires a page to state sharp or sandy drainage with no wet tolerance. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Plumbago; the page carries "Previously known as Plumbago capensis," and the unrelated Ceratostigma plumbaginoides is sold as "hardy plumbago," a different genus that must not be conflated with this tender one. Capture toxicity specifics as stated: the plant is generally reported to cause skin irritation or blistering from sap contact, and the sticky glandular calyces are a handling nuisance, so record the contact warning and any cat/dog scoping exactly rather than generalizing. Enum trap: it is drought-tolerant and prefers well-drained soil, but soil_drainage fast belongs only where a page specifies sharp or sandy drainage with no wet tolerance, and moisture_retentive is clearly wrong here. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This would be the catalog's fourth Ficus after benjamina, elastica and lyrata, and the only creeping one — take no size, light or watering data from those tree records. Capture the milky-latex handling warning (skin irritation on pruning) separately from the cat/dog ingestion toxicity, and record any statement about its aerial roots damaging walls or trim as a cultivation caution. Note the juvenile indoor foliage differs sharply from the mature fruiting form some pages describe. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

The corpus holds Asparagus officinalis as the edible vegetable, so this record must say plainly that A. setaceus is not that plant: capture the berry toxicity and the sap/spine dermatitis warning with their cat and dog scoping, and carry over no edibility statement. It is not a fern despite the name, and NC State keeps a separate page for Asparagus densiflorus (Sprengeri Group) — do not merge the two species' care. Set moisture_retentive only on an explicit cultivation requirement for consistently moist soil. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

The catalog's only Philodendron is hederaceum, so land this as Blushing Philodendron and source nothing from that record. Nearly all retail material describes the cultivars 'Pink Princess' and 'Imperial Red' — pull light, size and growth-habit data only from species-level text, never from a cultivar page. Capture the calcium-oxalate toxicity with its cat/dog scoping and any separate human handling or sap warning. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Clivia. Skip the outdated alias "Kaffir Lily" entirely and watch "Flame Lily", which properly belongs to Gloriosa superba; lead with Clivia or Bush Lily. Capture the lycorine toxicity with its cat and dog scoping plus any statement that the fleshy root base is the most toxic part, and record the cool dry winter rest as the cultivation condition that flowering depends on rather than as a watering preference. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Alchemilla; the synonyms Alchemilla acutiloba var. mollis and A. montana appear on older sources, and plants sold as A. mollis are often lumped under the A. vulgaris aggregate — do not merge an A. vulgaris page into this record. Capture any self-seeding or spread note and any herbal-use or edibility statement exactly as worded with its conditions rather than paraphrasing it into a general claim. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

The corpus holds Dianthus barbatus as Sweet William, and 'pinks' is shared with D. plumarius, D. deltoides and D. caryophyllus, so none of those pages may be used; the epithet also turns up as the synonym D. caesius. Toxicity is scoped to cats and dogs with mild GI upset plus a dermatitis risk from handling — record the cat/dog scoping and the handling warning as separate claims exactly as the source states them. This is the rare genuine fast case: it demands sharp, gritty, alkaline drainage with no wet tolerance, and moisture_retentive is flatly wrong. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

Cosmos bipinnatus is landed as Cosmos, so lead with Sulphur Cosmos (the pages also give Klondike Cosmos and Orange Cosmos) and keep the two records distinct in name, height and flower color. This is a lean-soil annual that flops in rich ground: do not set moisture_retentive, and reserve soil_drainage fast for an explicit sharp or sandy requirement with no wet tolerance. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

Landed Capsicum annuum is "Pepper," and this is a separate species whose content must be gathered fresh rather than inherited from it. NC State's name list leads with Carolina Reaper, which is a cultivar, so take species-level traits only and let no cultivar text stand in for the species. Capsaicin belongs in a handling warning about skin and eye contact when cutting, not in a poisonous-to-humans claim, unless the dedicated page states a toxicity section of its own. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

Landed Phaseolus vulgaris is "Green Beans" and this is a different species, so build the record independently. Toxicity is conditional and must be captured with its conditions: hydrocyanic acid in roots and seeds, the page's statement that it may be fatal if eaten raw, that the toxin is destroyed by thorough cooking, and that mature seed should be soaked twelve hours and cooked thoroughly while immature seed can simply be cooked like peas. Never reduce that to a bare edible flag. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Pastinaca. The page's own name list runs Parsnip through Wild Parsnip, and the plant is routinely confused with landed Conium maculatum (Poison Hemlock) and with carrot foliage, so state the distinction rather than leaving it. Toxicity must be recorded in full: furanocoumarins, Causes Contact Dermatitis yes, poison parts including sap/juice, symptoms of light-sensitised skin leading to severe burns and blisters, and the page's explicit instruction to wear protective equipment when handling; edibility is limited to the fleshy first-year taproot. Its drainage list includes Occasionally Wet, which rules out soil_drainage fast. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

Parthenocissus quinquefolia (Virginia Creeper) is landed and is the constant confusion here — Boston ivy has three-lobed leaves, not five leaflets, and clings by adhesive pads that damage some surfaces differently. It is also not an ivy at all, so do not let Hedera helix facts (also landed) bleed in. Capture toxicity specifically: berries carry oxalate crystals and are reported toxic to people and pets, and sap can irritate skin, so record the handling warning with the ingestion warning. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

Pinus strobus and P. taeda are landed as forest trees, so keep the shrub habit and the candle-pruning maintenance facts scoped strictly to mugo; note also that most plants sold are dwarf selections and that ungrafted seedlings can outgrow their label badly. Toxicity is usually reported as low, but capture the pet scoping and any sap or needle handling notes as the pages give them, and be careful with the drainage enum: well-drained is not soil_drainage fast unless the page calls for sandy or sharply drained soil with no wet tolerance. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.

This catalog's first Cotinus. Traps: it is sold as both smoketree and smokebush and is confused with the native American smoketree Cotinus obovatus, and the purple-leaved 'Royal Purple' and 'Grace' pages describe cultivars, not the species. Because it is in the Anacardiaceae with the landed sumacs (Rhus aromatica, R. typhina), capture any sap or contact-dermatitis handling warning exactly, along with the pet-toxicity scoping as the pages word it. Confirm species-specific content on a dedicated single-species page, never a genus-level, cultivar, or multi-species page.
